full_title: JANITO M. SEDENIO, PETITIONER, VS. PEOPLE OF THE PHILIPPINES, RESPONDENT.
subject: Criminal Law
syllabus_topic: IV. Special Penal Laws > Q. Anti-Violence Against Women and Their Children Act (RA 9262, Secs. 3–6 and 24–27)
topics: Violence against women through harassment (Sec. 5(h)(5), RA 9262): elements
Present or past dating or sexual relationship; information need not allege the relationship had ended
Victim's credible testimony suffices to prove alarm or substantial emotional distress
Proof of text messages under the Rules on Electronic Evidence; judicial admission
Rule 45 defects: no proof of service on the lower court; incomplete material dates

other_subjects.subject: Remedial Law, Legal and Judicial Ethics
other_subjects.syllabus_topic: VIII. Evidence > E. Kinds (Rule 130) > 2. Documentary Evidence > e. Electronic Evidence (AM 01-7-01-SC)

doctrine:
Violence against women through harassment under **Section 5(h)(5) of RA 9262** has three elements (reiterated, Ang v. CA). (1) The offender has or had a sexual or dating relationship with the offended woman. (2) The offender, personally or through another, commits an act or series of acts of harassment against her. (3) The harassment causes her alarm or substantial emotional or psychological distress. The first element is met **as long as, at the time of the crime, the offender and the woman were or used to be in a sexual or dating relationship.** A clandestine affair between two people married to others qualifies. The Information need not allege that the relationship had already ended when the Information was filed; that fact is immaterial.

**Proof that the victim became psychologically ill is not required. Whether she suffered alarm or substantial emotional or psychological distress is personal to her, so her testimony, if found credible, is sufficient to prove the third element** (applying Araza v. People). No psychological report or expert testimony is needed.

Text messages are proved by the testimony of a person who was a party to them or has personal knowledge of them (Rules on Electronic Evidence, Rule 11, Sec. 2). The recipient's testimony suffices. The accused's admission in open court that the sending number was his and that he sent the "humiliating [and] threatening" messages is a judicial admission. It binds him absent palpable mistake or proof that no such admission was made (Rule 129, Sec. 4). A Rule 45 petition that lacks proof of service on the lower court or omits material dates may be dismissed on that ground alone (Rule 45, Secs. 3-5).
facts:
Petitioner Janito Sedenio was charged under Section 5(h)(5) of RA 9262. The Information alleged that from February to August 2012, in Negros Oriental, he sent threatening and derogatory text messages to AAA, "with whom accused has a dating relationship," causing her alarm and substantial emotional or psychological distress.

Sedenio, a project engineer, met AAA in 2009 and they began a relationship. Both testified that it was a clandestine romantic relationship of about two years even though both were married to other people. Sedenio paid the amortization on AAA's housing unit. The relationship soured in 2011, after a dispute over a sugarcane harvest and after AAA told him about another man, YYY. Sedenio then sent her a series of text messages. On July 18, 2012, he threatened to humiliate her before her creditors and called her irresponsible and of ill repute. On July 20, 2012, he demanded payment of PHP 20,000.00 and wrote, "If you will ignore me, just wait for what I will do. I will include your consenting mother." On July 23, 2012, he accused her of embezzling money from the lending company where she worked. On August 2, 2012, he sent a vulgar message about YYY. On August 13, 2012, he forcibly entered her house using a kitchen knife. After that he sent mocking messages. In them he said she humiliated herself by calling the police, called her dumb, threatened to file a blotter against her, and threatened to show everyone a photo of the two of them in bed without clothes. AAA testified that she suffered mental anguish, sleepless nights for about six months, and a besmirched reputation, and that she could no longer look her neighbors in the eye.

Sedenio admitted the relationship. He also admitted on cross-examination that the sending number was his. He said that, hurt by AAA's relationship with YYY and sometimes drunk, he sent her "humiliating [and] threatening words."

The RTC (February 11, 2022) convicted him and imposed an indeterminate penalty of six months and one day of *prision correccional* to eight years and one day of *prision mayor*, a PHP 100,000.00 fine, mandatory psychological counseling, and PHP 3,000.00 moral damages. The CA affirmed on May 17, 2023 and denied reconsideration on July 15, 2024. In his Rule 45 petition, Sedenio argued the following. The text messages were never presented in court and authenticated under the Rules on Electronic Evidence. Intent to harass was not proved. The Information failed to state that their relationship had ended when it was filed. The victim's testimony alone, without a psychological expert or other witnesses, could not prove emotional distress.
issues: Whether the petition is dismissible for non-compliance with the requirements of Rule 45.
Whether the text messages were sufficiently proven.
Whether the Information was defective for not alleging that petitioner and AAA were no longer in a relationship when it was filed.
Whether the elements of violation of Section 5(h)(5) of RA 9262 were proven beyond reasonable doubt, including alarm or substantial emotional or psychological distress without expert evidence.
ruling:
**1. The petition was procedurally defective.** A petition for review must be accompanied by proof of service on the adverse party and on the lower court concerned (Rule 45, Sec. 3). It must also state the material dates: receipt of the assailed judgment, filing of the motion for reconsideration, and receipt of its denial (Sec. 4). Non-compliance is sufficient ground for dismissal (Sec. 5). Petitioner served the OSG but attached no proof of service on the CA. Although he attached the CA Decision and his motion for reconsideration, he did not state when he received the Decision or when he filed the motion. In any case, the Court found no reversible error on the merits.

**2. Yes, the text messages were sufficiently proven.** Under the Rules on Electronic Evidence, text messages are proved by the testimony of a person who was a party to them or has personal knowledge of them. AAA, the intended recipient, testified on the messages. Petitioner himself admitted that the mobile number was his and that he sent AAA "humiliating [and] threatening words" because he felt hurt and was often drunk. **He cannot go back on this judicial admission, there being no showing of palpable mistake or that the admission was not made.**

**3. No, the Information was sufficient.** The first element is "either a present or past sexual or dating relationship." **"[A]s long as at the time the alleged crime was committed, the offender and the offended woman either were or used to be in a sexual or dating relationship, the foregoing element is present."** The Information alleged a dating relationship at the time of the offense and the sending of threatening and derogatory messages that caused AAA distress. Whether they were still in a relationship when the Information was filed is immaterial. Petitioner was sufficiently informed of the nature and cause of the accusation.

**4. Yes, all elements were proven.** (a) Both parties testified to a clandestine romantic relationship of about two years though both were married to others. (b) AAA's testimony and petitioner's judicial admission established a series of harassing text messages from July to August 2012. As the CA put it, what the law punishes is engaging in purposeful, knowing, or reckless conduct that causes psychological harm, and petitioner knowingly and purposefully sent the messages. (c) Harassment is a form of psychological violence (RA 9262, Sec. 3(a)(C)). Araza v. People held that proof that the victim became psychologically ill is not required, and her testimony suffices to prove emotional anguish or mental suffering. **Likewise, whether a victim experienced alarm or substantial emotional or psychological distress "is an experience that is particular to her. Hence, her testimony—if found credible by the court—is sufficient."** The messages threatened to humiliate AAA before creditors, threatened her and her mother, accused her of embezzlement, mocked her for calling the police, and threatened to show a nude photo of them in bed. AAA testified to mental anguish, about six months of sleepless nights, and a besmirched reputation.

On the penalty, Section 6 of RA 9262 punishes Section 5(h) acts with *prision mayor*. Applying the Indeterminate Sentence Law, with no modifying circumstance, the penalty imposed by the courts below was affirmed. The fine, moral damages, and mandatory counseling were also affirmed (Secs. 6 and 36), with 6% legal interest per annum on the moral damages from finality until full payment.
disposition: The Petition was DENIED. The CA Decision of May 17, 2023 and Resolution of July 15, 2024 in CA-G.R. CR No. 04105 were AFFIRMED with MODIFICATION. Sedenio was found GUILTY beyond reasonable doubt of violating Section 5(h)(5) of RA 9262 and sentenced to an indeterminate penalty of six months and one day of *prision correccional*, as minimum, to eight years and one day of *prision mayor*, as maximum. He was ordered to pay a fine of PHP 100,000.00 and moral damages of PHP 3,000.00, the latter with 6% legal interest per annum from finality until full payment. He was directed to undergo mandatory psychological counseling or psychiatric treatment and to report compliance to the court of origin within 15 days from its completion.

bar_questions.q: After Bea ended her two-year relationship with Carlo, he sent her dozens of text messages over three months. He called her a thief, threatened to post their intimate photos for her neighbors to see, and warned that she and her mother would "pay." Charged under Section 5(h)(5) of RA 9262, Carlo argued that the prosecution presented no psychologist or medical report to prove that Bea suffered emotional distress, only Bea's own testimony that she could not sleep for months and was ashamed to face her neighbors. The trial court found Bea credible. Is Bea's testimony sufficient to prove the element of substantial emotional or psychological distress?

alac.answer: Yes. Bea's credible testimony is sufficient; no psychological report or expert testimony is required.
alac.legal_basis: The elements of Section 5(h)(5) of RA 9262 are: (1) the offender has or had a sexual or dating relationship with the woman; (2) he commits an act or series of acts of harassment against her; and (3) the harassment causes her alarm or substantial emotional or psychological distress. Proof that the victim became psychologically ill is not required. Whether she suffered alarm or substantial emotional or psychological distress is particular to her, so her testimony, if credible, is sufficient (Sedenio v. People, G.R. No. 276927, January 19, 2026, applying Araza v. People).
alac.application: Carlo and Bea had a past dating relationship. His repeated messages calling her a thief, threatening to expose intimate photos, and warning that she and her mother would "pay" are a series of acts of harassment. Bea testified to sleepless nights and shame before her neighbors, experiences personal to her, and the court found her credible. Nothing more is needed to prove the third element.
alac.conclusion: Bea's testimony suffices, and Carlo may be convicted under Section 5(h)(5) of RA 9262.

bar_questions.q: Dina and Edgar, both married to other people, carried on a secret affair for two years. Two months after Dina ended it, Edgar began sending her threatening and insulting text messages that caused her serious anxiety. The Information alleged that Edgar sent the messages to Dina, "with whom he had a dating relationship." Edgar moves to quash. He argues that (a) an adulterous affair cannot be a "dating relationship" under RA 9262, and (b) the Information is defective because it does not allege that the relationship had already ended when the Information was filed. Rule on both arguments.

alac.answer: Both arguments fail. (a) The affair is a sexual or dating relationship under RA 9262. (b) The Information need not allege that the relationship had ended when it was filed.
alac.legal_basis: The first element of Section 5(h)(5) of RA 9262 is that the offender "has or had" a sexual or dating relationship with the woman. It is present as long as, at the time of the crime, they were or used to be in such a relationship. Whether they were still in a relationship when the Information was filed is immaterial (Sedenio v. People, G.R. No. 276927, January 19, 2026). In Sedenio, the Court treated a clandestine two-year relationship between persons married to others as satisfying this element.
alac.application: (a) Edgar and Dina had a two-year romantic relationship. That both were married to others does not take it outside RA 9262, as Sedenio shows. (b) The messages were sent after the relationship ended, but a past relationship suffices. The Information alleges a dating relationship and the harassing acts, which informs Edgar of the nature and cause of the accusation. The status of the relationship at the time of filing is not an element and need not be alleged.
alac.conclusion: The motion to quash should be denied on both grounds.

bar_questions.q: In a prosecution under RA 9262, the private complainant testified on the contents of the threatening text messages she received and identified handwritten transcriptions of them, but the cellphone itself was not presented. On cross-examination, the accused admitted that the sending number was his and that he sent the complainant "insulting and threatening" messages because he was hurt. On appeal, he argues that the text messages are inadmissible because they were never presented and authenticated in court as ephemeral electronic communications. (a) How are text messages proved under the Rules on Electronic Evidence? (b) What is the effect of the accused's testimony?

alac.answer: (a) Text messages are proved by the testimony of a person who was a party to them or who has personal knowledge of them. (b) The accused's testimony is a judicial admission that binds him.
alac.legal_basis: Under Rule 11, Section 2, in relation to Rule 2, Section 1(k), of the Rules on Electronic Evidence, ephemeral electronic communications such as text messages are proved by the testimony of a person who was a party to them or has personal knowledge of them. Under Rule 129, Section 4 of the Rules of Court, a judicial admission does not require proof. It may be contradicted only by showing that it was made through palpable mistake or that no such admission was made (Sedenio v. People, G.R. No. 276927, January 19, 2026).
alac.application: (a) The complainant was the recipient of the messages, a party to them with personal knowledge of their contents. Her testimony is the proof the Rules require; presentation of the phone itself is not indispensable. (b) The accused admitted in open court that the number was his and that he sent insulting and threatening messages. He shows no palpable mistake, so he cannot later deny authorship. Together, the complainant's testimony and his admission sufficiently prove the messages.
alac.conclusion: The text messages were sufficiently proven, and the accused is bound by his judicial admission.

notes: No separate opinions. The private offended party is anonymized as AAA (and third persons as YYY, KKK, etc.) per Amended Administrative Circular No. 83-2015; the digest keeps that anonymization. The facts portion of the E-Library text contains an apparent typographical error ("Negros Negros Occidental") while the Information and the RTC refer to Negros Oriental. The penalty computation is stated only as affirmed; per the exam rules, penalty periods are not tested.
